Event_Names: Winter Storm in the Midwestern United States
Time_Annotation: The article notes that 'Interstate 65 in the northern part of the state was shut down for a short period on March 2' and later that 'several inches of sleet fell across the state, which prompted government buildings, schools, businesses, and colleges to close on March 3.'
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Locations mentioned include: 'In Kentucky, the roof of a Dollar General collapsed in Mayfield, Kentucky' and 'roads in the state were covered in ice'; 'In Indiana, numerous traffic accidents were reported around Indianapolis and New Albany, with 9.8 inches of snow falling in Portage'; 'In Tennessee, governor Bill Haslam declared a state of emergency with closures on March 3'; 'In Ohio, snow emergencies were in effect and the John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge was closed due to ice'; 'In Illinois, the highest snow total was 5.5 inches near Hillsdale'; and 'in Missouri, 5 inches of sleet was reported in Dudley and Pemiscot County.'
Main_Event_Annotation: The widespread winter disruptions — including record snowfall (9.8 inches in Portage, Indiana) and multiple roadway and infrastructure impacts across several states — indicate a severe extratropical storm/cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: While heavy snow, sleet, and icy conditions are described, the text does not explicitly mention hazards such as wind, flood, blizzard, or hail as outlined in the Main_Event–Hazard association table.

Total_Summary_Affected.Total_Affected_Annotation: In Arkansas, 4.5 inches (11 cm) of sleet fell at Biggers, in which the ice and sleet caused accidents along Interstate 40 and Interstate 55, causing motorists to be stranded overnight.[15]; The sleet and ice in Louisiana caused a 60 miles (97 km) closure along Interstate 10 between Lafayette and Lake Charles, where some Mardi Gras events were canceled; During Mardi Gras festivities in New Orleans, temperatures were as low as 39°F (4°C) on the afternoon of March 4, the second-most coldest Mardi Gras event in New Orleans on record, 1 degree shy of 38°F (3°C), which was set in 1899. Attendance was also lowered at the event, and the parade was shortened for high school and college units, which included dozens of bands.[28]; In Texas, 2 inches (5.1 cm) of sleet fell in Quitman and Van, which caused power outages, with 7,100 power outages in the Houston area.[15]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In Arkansas, 4.5 inches (11 cm) of sleet fell at Biggers,[1] in which the ice and sleet caused accidents along Interstate 40 and Interstate 55, causing motorists to be stranded overnight.[15]
The sleet and ice in Louisiana caused a 60 miles (97 km) closure along Interstate 10 between Lafayette and Lake Charles, where some Mardi Gras events were canceled.

During Mardi Gras festivities in New Orleans, temperatures were as low as 39°F (4°C) on the afternoon of March 4, the second-most coldest Mardi Gras event in New Orleans on record, 1 degree shy of 38°F (3°C), which was set in 1899. Attendance was also lowered at the event, and the parade was shortened for high school and college units, which included dozens of bands.[28]
In Texas, 2 inches (5.1 cm) of sleet fell in Quitman and Van,[1] which caused power outages, with 7,100 power outages in the Houston area.[15]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The main storm traveled from Daykin to a point south‐southeast of Western and then about 2 miles north of Swanton. During this phase, while fluctuating between F0 and F1 intensity, it damaged farmhouses and silos.
The tornado remained within the F0-F1 range until it hit southern Wilber, where it intensified to F2 and blew roofs off of structures.
At Hallam, the tornado became violent, reaching high-end F4 intensity at 8:35 pm CDT. Most houses were completely demolished, along with other structures, and a coal train was tossed off its tracks.
Norris School District 160 suffered severe damage: the middle school was hit hard, with the auditorium roof and other walls caving in, buses tossed, and homes northeast of the school flattened.

Time_Annotation: At 18:00 UTC on 28 August, a tropical depression formed just to the east of the Northern Mariana Islands. Later, key time markers include the system attaining tropical storm intensity by 00:00 UTC on 31 August, reaching typhoon intensity by 00:00 UTC on 1 September, making landfall on Fujian, China before 00:00 UTC on 7 September, and finally striking South Chungcheong Province in the Republic of Korea shortly after 06:00 UTC on 9 September with dissipation six hours later.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text states that the tropical depression formed just to the east of the Northern Mariana Islands, passed over the south tip of Guam, made landfall on Fujian in China, and later struck South Chungcheong Province in the Republic of Korea.
Main_Event_Annotation: The narrative describes the system evolving from a tropical depression to Tropical Storm Cora and then intensifying into Typhoon Cora, which falls under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Multiple parts of the text highlight extreme wind conditions – for example, the rapid increase in maximum sustained winds from 85 mph to 145 mph, prolonged periods with wind speeds between 160–175 mph, and peak winds of 175 mph – clearly indicating wind as the primary hazard.

The worst damage occurred on Miyako-jima; the storm also damaged 1,400 homes, leaving 2,363 people homeless.

On nearby Ishigaki Island, a further 139 homes were severely damaged.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: By 4:30 p.m. CDT, a thunderstorm spawned an F3 tornado about 10 mi south of Rochester, near Pleasant Grove. The tornado killed two people, injured ten others, and damaged at least four farmsteads, one of which it destroyed.

The Rochester tornado first touched down at about 6:30 p.m. CDT (23:30 UTC) near Hayfield in Dodge County. It damaged farmsteads in Westfield, Hayfield, Ashland, Vernon, and Canisteo townships. In all, the tornado passed through 40 farms across Dodge County, at least 10 of which it razed.

As it entered Olmsted County, the tornado obliterated farmhouses, outbuildings, and machinery in Salem Township, causing one death. (Building damage is noted but no numerical count is provided for structures.)
The tornado continued to destroy structures on farms in Kalmar, Cascade, and Rochester townships before entering the city of Rochester itself, with no explicit count provided.

In just five minutes, the tornado passed through the north side of Rochester, causing devastating damage. The northern third of Rochester was devastated, with 135 homes destroyed and 200 damaged. The tornado also caused extensive damage to a 1-mile-wide swath that extended 10 mi eastward from Rochester.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: community garden center and two homes leveled; dozens of other nearby homes damaged
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Still rapidly strengthening, the tornado entered Grissettown and struck the Ocean Ridge Plantation subdivision at its peak intensity of high-end EF3. A community garden center and two homes were leveled at this location, one of which was swept completely away. Dozens of other nearby homes were damaged, some of which sustained loss of roofs and exterior walls. Many large trees were snapped and denuded in the subdivision, and a car was overturned.

The tornado then abruptly weakened but reached its maximum width as it crossed US 17 between Grissettown and Cool Run as it exited Ocean Ridge Plantation at EF1 strength, rolling a double-wide mobile home on the north side of the highway.
As the tornado continued northeast, it reintensifed to EF2 strength, causing major damage to several homes and snapping hundreds of trees.

Total_Summary_Deaths.Total_Deaths_Annotation: All three fatalities occurred in the Ocean Ridge Plantation subdivision. Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: One strong tornado, rated EF2, moved through Hopkinsville, Kentucky, damaging several businesses, homes, warehouses, a church, and a gas station.[16][17]

A weak EF0 tornado embedded within larger area straight-line winds also caused minor damage in Bowling Green, an area previously impacted by two strong tornadoes during the previous month, which killed 16 people and injured 63 others.[18][19]
An EF1 tornado damaged a few homes, destroyed barns, downed trees, and knocked over gravestones at a cemetery in the Hiseville, Kentucky area.
Another brief EF1 tornado caused damage to a few metal buildings and garages at the east edge Lebanon, Kentucky.
Near Hazel Green, Alabama, a high-end EF0 tornado damaged several businesses, snapped tree branches, and ripped the roof off a mobile home.
Two weak tornadoes also touched down in North Carolina during the morning hours of January 3 before the outbreak ended, one of which caused EF1 damage to some hog barns near Newton Grove.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: An EF3 tornado caused major damage to homes and school buildings in the city of Jacksboro, Texas, and destroyed some wind turbines and metal truss towers outside of town, injuring nine people.

The same supercell produced an EF2 tornado in Sherwood Shores, Texas, that caused major damage to homes, destroyed mobile homes, killed one person, and injured 11 others before crossing the state line.
After impacting Sherwood Shores, the tornado crossed the state line and caused severe damage at the Buncombe Creek Marina near Kingston, Oklahoma.
Two EF1 tornadoes caused considerable damage near Bowie, Texas, and injured three people.
A high-end EF2 tornado flipped cars and caused major damage to homes and businesses in the Austin suburb of Round Rock, as well as in areas to the northeast, injuring 16 others.
Later that evening, an EF2 tornado touched down in and around Crockett, Texas, where multiple homes and a convenience store suffered major structural damage.
Another strong tornado produced high-end EF2 damage near Ore City, destroying homes and mobile homes and injuring seven people.
Other strong EF2 tornadoes occurred near the towns of Kingsbury, Elgin and Cushing.
An EF3 tornado struck rural Kemper County, Mississippi in the Damascus area, producing severe tree damage and destroying a couple of homes.

A strong multiple-vortex EF3 tornado caused major damage in the New Orleans metropolitan area, with the most severe damage occurring in the inner suburb of Arabi, where many homes were destroyed and vehicles tossed.
On March 23, one of the EF2 tornadoes caused significant damage near Pickens, South Carolina.
On March 23, one of the EF2 tornadoes caused significant damage near Gladesboro, Virginia.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Tornadic activity began with an EF1 tornado northwest of Van Tassel, Wyoming, which damaged fences and farm buildings and produced a measured wind gust of 78 mph (126 km/h).[79][96]
Several weak tornadoes touched down in southern Nebraska and northern Kansas on the night of June 7, including an EF1 tornado that downed trees and damaged a grain bin in Narka, Kansas.[97][98][99]

An EF2 tornado near Buckner, Missouri, heavily damaged a metal building, tore a large section of roof off a house, and snapped or uprooted trees.[100]

An EF1 tornado downed numerous trees in and around Springfield, and caused minor damage to homes and outbuildings.
EF0 tornadoes caused minor damage in the towns of Sardinia, Ohio, and Summitville, Indiana, as well.

Farther east, a brief tornado caused EF0 damage near Mechanicsville, Maryland.
On June 9, two final weak tornadoes occurred along the East Coast, including an EF1 tornado that damaged trees, homes, a fence, and a shed near Blackwood, New Jersey.
Farther south, the other tornado produced EF0 damage to trees and structures in Port St. Lucie, Florida.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: 1 cell phone tower completely destroyed and several warehouses damaged
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The tornado entered the southern portion of Tuscaloosa as a low-end EF4 and crossed 35th Street, completely destroying a cell phone tower and several warehouses in an industrial area.
The Tuscaloosa County Emergency Management Office sustained a direct hit and was totally destroyed along with most of their equipment and vehicles, though no injuries were reported.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: numerous poorly-anchored homes leveled, several apartment complexes entirely destroyed, and a few two-story apartment buildings reduced to rubble
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The tornado ripped through the neighborhoods of Rosedale and Forest Lake, leveling and sweeping away numerous poorly-anchored homes. Several apartment complexes were entirely destroyed, and a few two‐story apartment buildings were reduced to rubble.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: numerous businesses and restaurants completely flattened
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The tornado crossed the intersection of 15th Street and McFarland Boulevard, and numerous businesses and restaurants near the University Mall were completely flattened at low‐end EF4 strength.
The nearby Cedar Crest subdivision was devastated as numerous block‐foundation homes were leveled.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: numerous block‐foundation homes leveled, two apartment buildings completely flattened, and a shopping center destroyed
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The tornado continued through the neighborhood of Alberta City, leveling and sweeping away numerous block‐foundation homes, and completely flattening two more apartment buildings and a shopping center along University Boulevard.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Chastain Manor Apartments completely destroyed and partially swept away; a well‐anchored clubhouse mostly swept away
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: As the tornado exited the Alberta City section, the Chastain Manor Apartments were completely destroyed and partially swept away, and a well‐anchored clubhouse on the property was mostly swept away with its remains scattered into a pond.

Time_Annotation: The origins of Tropical Storm Kelly can be traced back to an area of disturbed weather that was first detected by weather satellite imagery on June 25. On July 5, the JTWC stopped monitoring the system as it had moved inland.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Tropical Storm Kelly moved ashore along the central Philippines, and later, late on July 4, Kelly made landfall 185 km south of Hanoi in Vietnam.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was classified as a tropical cyclone when the JTWC upgraded the depression into Tropical Storm Kelly at 0600 UTC on June 30, and it was tracked as a tropical storm as it moved ashore.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind-related observations are noted with the Dvorak classification at T2.5 (65 km/h), surface observations from the Paracel Islands indicating winds of 134 km/h (83 mph), and the JTWC reporting a peak wind speed of 135 km/h (85 mph).

Time_Annotation: A persistent low-pressure area south of Kusaie was first noted on March 14; the remnants tracked westward before dissipating after 0600 UTC on March 28.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precursor system moved near Kusaie producing 137 mm of rain, passed to the south of Kwajalein where strong surface winds and 236 mm of rain were observed, and later threatened Wake Island and Eniwetok Atoll.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system steadily intensified—attaining tropical storm strength and then, at 0600 UTC on March 20, Georgia reached typhoon intensity—indicating a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The cyclone produced high winds (e.g., 185 km/h and gusts exceeding 95 km/h) and heavy rainfall (with peak totals of 137 mm and 236 mm reported), consistent with wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: The article states: '...developed into a tropical depression near Micronesia early on April 15.' and later mentions that 'the China Meteorological Agency (CMA)... determined that Hope had persisted up until late on April 23 before dissipating.'

Main_Event_Annotation: The disturbance intensified into a tropical storm and then a typhoon, as noted by the Guam Fleet Warning Center, which categorizes it as a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The article mentions that Hope reached its peak intensity with maximum sustained winds of 130 km/h (81 mph), indicating a wind hazard associated with tropical cyclones.
